analysis.one_liner: Has the federal government take over retiree health and life benefits for steelworkers whose companies closed or went bankrupt.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 16 senators including both a Democrat and Republicans, never received a committee vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: After surges of imported steel, dozens of American steel companies went bankrupt and more than 100,000 retirees lost their medical and life insurance benefits. This bill would have created a government-run program to restore those benefits, funded by steel tariffs, company asset transfers, and company contributions. It was also designed to help the steel industry consolidate by letting companies shed their retiree obligations when they were bought, closed, or went bankrupt.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired steelworkers and their spouses and dependents whose medical and life insurance was cut off when their companies went bankrupt or shut down. Steel companies and their acquirers also benefit, because once a qualifying event is certified the United States takes over the retiree benefit liability and the companies are relieved of it, which makes buying or restructuring distressed steelmakers easier. Retirees get coverage comparable to the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan available to federal employees, plus a $5,000 death benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Steel Industry Retiree Benefits Protection Program that provides medical, hospital, and death benefits to eligible steel retirees and beneficiaries, patterned on the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan in the Federal Employees Health Benefit Program.

When a qualifying event occurs — an acquisition, closing, election, or bankruptcy transfer — the United States assumes liability for providing those retiree benefits, and the company and its successors are relieved of that liability.

The bill's own findings state that since 1997, 32 American steel companies had entered bankruptcy, over 45,000 steelworkers had lost their jobs, and over 100,000 retirees had suffered a complete cutoff of vital medical and life insurance benefits.

Steel companies cannot simply walk away: they must transfer to a new trust fund any assets set aside for retiree benefits, and pay $5 per ton of steel shipped for 10 years, plus an amount equal to the accounting value of the retiree obligations they shed.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, because Congress is authorized to appropriate money each year to cover any gap between the trust fund's spending and its assets. Buyers of steel also bear a cost, since the fund is fed by steel tariffs paid into the Treasury and the companies' $5-per-ton contributions are tied to steel shipments. Steel companies themselves pay through required asset transfers and contributions, but the bill lets bankruptcy courts discharge part of that liability and lets an industry-wide election extinguish it.

drawbacks.text: The fund is not self-financing: the bill authorizes a yearly appropriation to cover any excess of program spending over the fund's assets, leaving an open-ended federal commitment.

Companies that go through bankruptcy can have their contribution liability reduced by whatever the bankruptcy proceeding discharges, so the weakest companies — and the ones whose retirees need help most — contribute the least.

If 200,000 retirees and beneficiaries are certified, an industry-wide election extinguishes all remaining company liability under the accounting-based formula and refunds prior payments with interest, shifting the full cost to the tariff- and taxpayer-backed fund.
The program covers only steel-industry retirees, raising the fairness question of why workers in other industries that lost retiree benefits get no comparable protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the retirees it targets, the bill restores a promise made over decades of work, at a cost funded partly by the companies themselves and partly by steel tariffs and a federal backstop. The main honest objections are that the taxpayer commitment is open-ended, the tariff funding raises costs for every downstream steel buyer, and the design rewards companies that shed obligations in bankruptcy. It is a targeted rescue, not a general retiree-benefit fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2002 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV introduced the bill on April 17, 2002, joined by eight other senators including Republican Arlen Specter and Democratic Majority Leader Tom Daschle.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors — 13 Senate Democrats and 2 Senate Republicans — but that support never translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, retired steelworkers who had lost their medical and life insurance got nothing from Congress. Steel buyers and taxpayers avoided the tariff-funded program, and steel companies that had already shed their retiree obligations in bankruptcy kept that advantage without taking on new obligations under this scheme.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 13 Senate Democrats were joined by 2 Senate Republicans, with the Democratic Majority Leader among the cosponsors, but no vote ever occurred in committee or on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have relieved steelmakers and companies buying their assets of retiree benefit obligations once a qualifying event was certified, easing consolidation of the industry — which the bill's findings call a goal. Companies paid through asset transfers and per-ton contributions, but bankruptcy discharge and an industry-wide election could wipe out much of that liability, leaving tariffs and taxpayers to cover the rest.

Over 100,000 retirees had lost medical and life insurance when their employers failed; the bill would have restored coverage at federal expense, administered by a board that included union designees alongside company designees.

The trust fund would be financed in part by steel tariffs collected in the Treasury and by per-ton charges tied to steel shipments, passing program costs into the price of steel for every downstream manufacturer and buyer.

industries.industry: Health insurers and preferred provider networks
industries.note: The trustee board would have contracted with insurers to deliver benefits modeled on the FEHBP Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan and could establish preferred provider networks, routing the new retiree program through private plans.
